paras: The Savannah wharf strike shooting was a confrontation on September 19, 1881, at the railroad bridge leading to the Central Railroad wharves in Savannah, Georgia, in which police sergeant H. H. Harvey was shot by someone in a crowd of Black striking laborers and police fired into the crowd. A squad of police with muskets then drove the strikers from the bridge, and no casualties among the crowd were confirmed. Harvey died of the wound a month later, and the strike brought out the city's militia.

On the morning of September 19 the Black laborers loading the steamship Gate City demanded a raise from $1.50 to $2 a day and left the wharf when H. M. Branch, who was in charge, said he could not answer until he saw the agent. The men gathered at the foot of the railroad bridge, where crowds of women from Cooper Shop lane joined them. The Savannah Morning News said the men had been drinking and called the women "exceedingly boisterous, vindictive and violent." A Richmond wire version placed the trouble on River street and blamed hands from the steamship Dessoug who came back drunk from dinner.

About 2:30 in the afternoon the crowd took possession of the bridge and stopped cotton drays from reaching the wharves. Summoned by telephone, Sergeant Harvey rode onto the bridge, two policemen following, and ordered the crowd to disperse. In both the local and the wire accounts a Black woman struck him on the leg with a stick, and when he jumped from his horse to seize her someone in the crowd fired a pistol, the ball passing about an inch below his heart.

Harvey drew his pistol and fired, and at least one other officer fired as well. The wire report said Harvey's two shots were "thought" to have wounded someone, while the Morning News said the result was unknown because any wounded men "succeeded in getting off." A squad of police with muskets and fixed bayonets, fifteen men in the local account and twenty in the wire, then arrived and the crowd scattered, many into the swamp. The man who shot Harvey was not identified and escaped.

The next day Chief of Police Anderson had an unnamed man the paper called a "ringleader" arrested at the bridge after he refused to give his name. The mayor assembled the Savannah Volunteer Guards and had the Chatham Artillery ready two guns with canister, though the day passed without serious disturbance. The Knights of Pythias, of which Harvey was a member, and other citizens proposed a reward for the arrest of the man who shot him.

Employers brought in new laborers under police guard, and on September 22, when strikers rushed a train carrying them, police charged the crowd and a wire report counted five Black men wounded. Three officers of the Black militia battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major Deveaux and Adjutant Toomer, urged the strikers to petition peaceably, while the governor and mayor issued proclamations.

Harvey died on October 19 of blood poisoning from a small bullet that physicians believed had lodged in his spine. Coroner Sheftall held an inquest, but the jury adjourned without a verdict, and no verdict, arrest or trial of the shooter appears in the coverage. Citizens met at Armory Hall the next day to raise a fund for his widow and child.

The Savannah Morning News treated the strike as a riot, blamed whisky and the Black women in the crowd, and called Harvey's assailant a "worthless negro." It said the troops had put the strikers "on notice," and on Harvey's death headlined "The Work of a Lawless Assassin."

Within a day the wire carried the story out of state as "Riotous Stevedores in Savannah" in the Richmond Daily Dispatch and "Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers" in the Anderson Intelligencer, which warned of "bloody work." The Weekly Floridian reprinted the Richmond version on September 27. None of these accounts gives the strikers' own version of the shooting.

Accounts of the crowd's losses differ: the Morning News did not know whether anyone was hit, the wire said someone was thought wounded, and Rhode Island's Burrillville Gazette claimed eight men killed and twelve wounded.

reader.title: Savannah wharf strike shooting
bases: Police fired into a crowd of Black strikers on the bridge and a musket squad with fixed bayonets drove them off after a sergeant was shot from the crowd during a wage strike (A1, A3); the setting is a labor dispute, but the force used against the Black crowd was by officers.

The local Savannah Morning News (A1) and two differently worded wire reports (A2, A3) agree on the strike, the bridge confrontation, the shooting of Harvey from the crowd and the police response; only the crowd's casualties are disputed (A12).

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News local report
accounts.gist: Drinking strikers and boisterous women seized the bridge; a woman struck Harvey with a stick, someone in the crowd shot him as he dismounted, he and one other officer fired with unknown result, and a musket squad cleared the bridge.

accounts.label: Wire report (Anderson Intelligencer)
accounts.gist: Same sequence at the canal bridge; Harvey fired two shots and 'it is thought wounded some one', other policemen opened fire, and twenty musket-armed police sent the crowd to the swamps.

accounts.label: Wire report (Richmond Dispatch)
accounts.gist: Drunken hands from the Dessoug blocked River street; Harvey was attacked by a crowd and shot by 'one of the mob'; reinforcements dispersed the rioters.

accounts.label: Rhode Island brief
accounts.gist: The stevedores' collision with police left eight men killed and twelve wounded.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called the strike a riot, blamed whisky and 'vindictive and violent' Black women, called the shooter a 'worthless negro', and approved troops with canister as putting the strikers 'on notice'.
Out-of-state papers ran the wire under 'Riotous Stevedores in Savannah' and 'Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers', warning of 'bloody work'.
On Harvey's death the local paper headlined 'The Work of a Lawless Assassin' and called him a martyr to duty.
